only part of the picture. Here’s how to stay sharp, mobile, and independent as you age. Longevity may be the wellness world’s new obsession, but many conversations about aging are missing the point. “It’s not about living to 100,” says Dr. Penny Stern , chief of preventive and lifestyle medicine at Northwell Health. “It’s about staying sharp, independent, and active—for as long as you’re here.” In other words, it’s about healthspan : The number of years you live with vitality and function, not just a heartbeat. And while influencers may tout supplements , hacks, and cryotherapy chambers, Stern argues that the most powerful ways to extend your healthspan are far simpler—and grounded in science. Here’s how she helps patients shift their focus from extra years to better ones—and the daily habits that can make that shift last a lifetime. It reflects the years you spend functioning well: moving with ease, thinking clearly , and participating in the activities that make life feel full. “Aging well isn’t about avoiding death,” Stern says. “It’s about protecting the quality of your life for as long as possible.” This shift in thinking changes everything. Instead of trying to add years, you’re trying to add vitality to the years you already have. And that comes from your daily behaviors, not your DNA. When researchers study centenarians—especially those who reach old age with their independence and cognition intact—there’s no single supplement, secret gene, or lifehack that emerges, but there are common threads. Stern follows these six core pillars of lifestyle medicine, a field that focuses on evidence-based changes that can prevent (and in some cases reverse) chronic disease. These include: “These aren’t quick fixes,” she says. “But they’re powerful, and they work.” While these habits stem from the six core pillars of lifestyle medicine—nutrition, movement, sleep , stress management, avoiding harmful substances, and social connection—Stern often expands her guidance to include mindset shifts and real-life strategies that help patients turn those pillars into lasting change. 1. Prioritize sleep as a health strategy “Sleep is foundational,” Stern says. “When you don’t sleep well, every other system in your body—your brain, your heart, your metabolism—suffers.” She advises aiming for seven to eight hours of uninterrupted sleep each night and treating bedtime as seriously as any wellness habit . That means limiting screens before bed, sticking to a routine, and avoiding caffeine and alcohol late in the day. “You can’t make up for poor sleep later,” she adds. “Sleep is like time, when it’s lost, it’s lost forever.” 2. Move your body—consistently and creatively One of the most overlooked brain-boosters? Walking . “You don’t need fancy equipment or a gym membership to support your healthspan,” says Stern. “Walking is accessible, safe, and incredibly effective.” Stern recommends 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity movement, ideally a mix of aerobic exercise and strength training. But even short bursts count. “A few minutes here and there add up,” she says. “And movement throughout the day is often more sustainable than trying to ‘make up for it’ on the weekends.” For those with mobility issues, physical activity is still essential. There are chair-based exercises, as well as other modalities. 3. Eat plants like your future depends on it Forget the fads. Stern points to plant-predominant, whole-food eating as one of the most consistent contributors to long-term vitality. “ Fiber , in particular, is crucial,” she says. “It helps regulate blood sugar , supports digestion, lowers LDL cholesterol, and helps you feel full longer.” The good news? High-fiber, high-nutrient foods like beans, oats, carrots, broccoli, bananas, and apples are often more affordable than the heavily marketed alternatives. “You don’t need to shop at specialty stores to eat for healthspan,” she says. “You just need to shop the perimeter of the grocery store.” 4. Be mindful of what you don’t eat Ultra-processed foods, added sugars , saturated fats, and excessive salt can quietly chip away at your healthspan. So can alcohol—especially when it interferes with sleep or becomes a default coping mechanism. Stern’s advice: “Read the labels . Know what’s in your food. If you see ingredients with five syllables you can’t pronounce, or a long list of additives, make other choices.” 5. Skip the supplements (unless your doctor says otherwise) Despite what you might see on TikTok, there’s no magic pill for healthspan. “Unless you have a diagnosed deficiency—like vitamin D or iron—your micronutrients should come from food,” Stern says. “Supplements aren’t well regulated, and you often don’t know what you’re really getting.” She also cautions against taking medical advice from influencers. “If someone is promising a miracle result—or selling you a solution—it’s usually a red flag.” 6. Strengthen your social ties “ Loneliness is as harmful to your health as smoking,” says Stern. “We’re not meant to age in isolation.” That doesn’t mean you need a large circle of friends or a traditional family structure. “Volunteering, group classes, mentorship, faith communities—there are many ways to stay connected,” she notes. “What matters most is feeling seen, valued, and engaged.” 7. Anchor your life in purpose Whether it’s a project, a routine, or a role you value, a sense of purpose can fuel physical and emotional resilience. “Patients who have something to wake up for tend to thrive,” Stern says. She points to her late father-in-law, who worked as a track and field coach until the age of 90. “He felt great and didn’t want to retire,” she shares. “That kind of drive and engagement—especially in later life—makes a difference.” 8. Manage stress like it matters (because it does) Chronic stress can disrupt sleep, spike inflammation, accelerate aging, and raise the risk of nearly every chronic disease. “You can’t eliminate stress,” Stern says. “But you can learn to manage it.” Her favorite go-to strategies include movement, meditation , yoga , spending time in nature , and simply talking to someone. “There’s no wrong way to manage stress, as long as it’s sustainable and helps you come back to yourself.” 9. Start small—and don’t wait for perfect conditions “You don’t need to do everything at once,” Stern says. “Healthspan is built on consistency, not intensity.” In fact, some of the most impactful shifts are free or low-cost: daily walking, home-cooked meals , better sleep, deeper friendships. “Pick one area to focus on, build momentum, and go from there,” she says. “Your future self will thank you.” Like what you’re reading?
